Red junglefowl (Gallus gallus) hatchlings emerge after an incubation period of 21 days [ab = 21 days] when eggs are maintained at 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C], a finding consistent with the thermal optimum required for embryonic development in Galliformes. Under standard husbandry conditions maintained at 41 °C [T = 41 °C], precocial chicks exhibit a wet body mass of 26.65 grams [Wwb = 26.65 grams] at hatching, and the fledging stage, marked by the achievement of coordinated flight and the ability to evade ground predators, occurs at just 3 days after hatching [tx = 3 days after hatching]; this abbreviated nestling phase is characteristic of precocial birds that forage alongside their parents almost immediately after yolk-sac resorption. Field observations confirm that this early independence imposes substantial selective pressure on juvenile foraging efficiency.

Juvenile birds progress through a distinct sub-adult phase before attaining reproductive capacity, with published accounts from captive colonies indicating that under the same thermal regime of 41 °C [T = 41 °C], puberty is reached at approximately 100 days after hatching [tp = approximately 100 days after hatching] and first breeding events occur at 174.3 days after hatching [tR = 174.3 days after hatching]. This timing coincides with the onset of gonadal maturation and the development of the species' characteristic sexual dichromatism. The delay between achieving sexual maturity and initiating a first clutch likely reflects the energetic demands of establishing a dominance hierarchy and securing a suitable territory within the dense understory habitats these birds occupy across their native range from the Himalayan foothills through Southeast Asia. Females in particular allocate substantial resources toward somatic growth during this interim period, as body mass continues to increase.

Adult body size exhibits pronounced sexual dimorphism in Red junglefowl, a trait that reflects divergent selective pressures on the sexes. Males attain an ultimate wet weight of 1200.0 grams [Wwi = 1200.0 grams], a figure consistent with the demands of intrasexual competition for access to hens and the energetic costs of maintaining ornamental plumage and comb tissue. Females, by contrast, reach a substantially lower asymptotic mass of 959.3 grams [Wwi = 959.3 grams], an adult size that balances the metabolic requirements of egg production with the necessity of cryptic mobility during incubation. These values, derived from long-term captive studies, align well with the range of 485 to 1050 grams reported for wild-caught individuals in the ARKive database, though natural populations exhibit greater variability driven by local resource availability and seasonal fluctuations in food abundance. Total body length from the tip of the beak to the terminus of the tail feathers also differs between the sexes.

Linear measurements further underscore the size disparity between males and females, with the ultimate total length of the species recorded at 57.0 centimeters [Li = 57.0 centimeters] in fully grown adult males; females are typically several centimeters shorter, a difference primarily attributable to the elongation of the central rectrices in males that serve as a signal of individual quality during courtship displays. This morphological trait, combined with the red comb and wattles that become fully developed after puberty, constitutes a critical component of mate choice in this lekking species. The reproductive output of a single breeding female, maintained under optimal thermal conditions at 41 °C [T = 41 °C], reveals a maximum rate achievable through the combination of clutch size and nesting frequency: a hen typically lays 3 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = 3 eggs per clutch], and under continuous favorable conditions, she can produce approximately 2 clutches each year [F_R_i = approximately 2 clutches each year], though wild populations rarely sustain this upper limit due to nest predation and seasonal resource bottlenecks.

Longevity records for Red junglefowl indicate a maximum lifespan of 9125 days [am = 9125 days] under captive conditions when birds are maintained at a constant 41 °C [T = 41 °C], a duration equivalent to roughly 25 years that places this species among the longer-lived Galliformes. In natural populations, however, mortality from predation, disease, and conspecific aggression drastically reduces median survivorship, with very few individuals reaching even half this potential age. The selective pressures imposed by a variable environment have shaped a life history where rapid juvenile development and iteroparity with relatively small clutch sizes (three eggs per clutch [N_R_i = three eggs per clutch]) facilitate a sustained reproductive effort across numerous breeding seasons. Ecological studies have demonstrated that this syndrome is tightly linked to the species' ability to colonize a wide variety of habitats, from primary rainforest to agricultural edges, where supplemental food resources can elevate chick survival. Comparative analyses with other Galliformes confirm that the parameters described here reflect a generalized strategy adapted to unpredictable resource environments.
